ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: the region
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: The towns within the region map's reach are known in detail: each has a fortune the world's events move, and a new one has a founder, founding families and a reason it stands where it does.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A town that has just been founded is poor for a while. Its founder writes to a colony nearby, and its people are glad of friends in their first year.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description:
Rimfolk keeps the towns near each of your homes in detail: the towns of humanlike peoples within the region map's reach (35 tiles by default, set in the settings from 20 to 60), the nearest 40 for each home. A town within reach of two homes is one town, with one fortune. Beyond the reach the game and other mods keep the world as they always have, and Rimfolk keeps nothing there and changes nothing there.
Every town in detail has a fortune, from 0 to 100, that the world's events move and that shows in its panel on the region map and in its people's words. A town founded within reach gets a face: someone of its people who led the settlers out, two founding families known by name, the town they came from and the reason they chose the place. The colony hears of it in the news, its founder writes when the town stands near enough, and its people talk of it.

li.heading: Fortunes
li.text: A town first seen starts at 50, up to 15 less on poor land (by its land's settlement weight, the game's own sense of where towns stand) and 10 less while its people are in hard times (a hard world event about them). A new town starts at 30, and a town taken in an invasion starts again at 25 under its new people.

table.li: Prosperity | In words
Under 20 | Struggling (a tribe's town is hungry, an industrial town short of everything)
20 to 39 | Poor (lean, for a tribe)
40 to 59 | Steady
60 to 79 | Thriving (prospering, for medieval folk)
80 or more | Flourishing (booming, for spacers)

li.after: Once a day, each town drifts back toward 50 (45 on poor land) by 0.3, a town within 20 tiles of a town of a people its own is at war with loses 0.3, and the world's events move it. Its panel names what moved it last, for 60 days, when that fits how it stands now: "Struggling, since the plague", "Thriving: the new road", "Poor: newly founded". Its people say the same when they talk of their town, and how it mends once a hard time or a war is over.

It shows in what the town sells, too. When the game restocks a town within reach, a struggling one has a quarter less food, medicine and silver to trade, a thriving one a tenth more silver and a flourishing one a fifth more; nothing else in its stock changes, and other mods' changes to the stock are made first (with the deeper game hooks).

li.heading: What the world's events do to a town
li.text: A world event about a people moves the town it happens at in full and that people's other towns in detail by half, a fifth of it on each of its first five days, so the change shows while it runs. A war of words between two creeds, a blood feud and markets closed against a people move the second people's towns too, each by half its number.

table.li: World event | Its town | Its people's other towns | The second people's towns
The great fire | -30 | -15 | none
Famine | -25 | -12.5 | none
Plague in the region | -20 | -10 | none
A locust swarm, a flood downriver, a long drought | -15 | -7.5 | none
A war of words | -15 | -7.5 | -7.5
A sickness in the herds | -12 | -6 | none
A hard winter, a merchant house fails | -10 | -5 | none
Bandit road | -8 | -4 | none
A contested seat | -6 | -3 | none
Blood feud | -6 | -3 | -3
Iron gone scarce | -5 | -2.5 | none
Markets closed | none | none | -5
A silver rush, gold fever | 12 | 6 | none
A bumper harvest, a trading season, a new road, rebuilding | 10 | 5 | none
A great fair, the road reopens, busy orbital lanes | 8 | 4 | none
Market days, the road in use, a bandit lord falls | 6 | 3 | none
A great pilgrimage, a ship comes down, an old vault opened, the ice road | 5 | 2.5 | none
A holy year | 4 | 2 | none

li.heading: New towns
li.text: A town begun or built within reach (by Faction Territories and Vassalage's builders, or by Rimfolk's own world events: a new town, other settlers, the crossroads) gets a founder soon after: someone of its people of their leaders' kind, aged 30 to 55, kept in the world while the town is known in detail (for the Empire, one of its titled kinds, so the title the news gives is the one the game shows). Two founders are made a day at most; a founding waits a day for one at most, then goes on without. With them come two founding families known by name (the founder's line and one more; where a people goes by family names, the town's envoy is born to the second), the town the settlers came from (their people's nearest other town), and a reason read from the land.

table.li: Reason | When
Families whose town was given up | A town of theirs was given up in the last 120 days
The old walls of a ruin | A ruin stands on the place or beside it
A crowded mother town | The town they came from is flourishing
The road, the river, the coast, the hills | The place has one
The land itself | Nothing else

li.after: The strongest reason that holds is the usual one, the others now and then. When the town stands, its founder is its head, and for its first year (60 days) the town is kept among the neighbours by name beside the nearest four (two new towns at most). Its people speak of who led them, where they came from, why they chose the place and how their first seasons go, and visitors of other peoples mention the new town near the colony.

li.heading: How the colony hears of it
li.text: The colony news has one line when a town is begun and one when it stands, by the colony's own means (word from a traveler, a rider's news, news on the radio, a comms relay's report) and in their people's way of founding (a new hearth lit before the elders, a charter read and a market cross raised, streets staked out, a charter filed and the first habitats sealed). Within reach, this line takes the place of Faction Territories' own message about the same town, so it comes once; when Rimfolk doesn't take the town, the mod's message comes as it always did. A town Rimfolk's own world events found is told by the event's letter.
li.after: A new town within 15 tiles of a home welcomes itself in full, at most once a year for each home and when a world event's slot is free: its letter tells of the town, and within a few days a runner comes to the gate to ask whether the settlers may count the colony among their friends, a neighbor's gift hoped for and remembered (silver carried out to the runner), timber wanted at a fair price; its traders and visitors follow. Otherwise the town is told in the news, and its founder writes, at most one letter a season to each home: who they are and where, why they came, what their people remember of the colony (the good turn they remember best, or a wrong they want no part of), the families who came first, in their people's own voice. The region map shows a town's fortune and founding in its panel, a town being built and its settlers, and for a home how remote it is.

li.heading: How remote a home is
li.text: Remoteness runs from 0 to 1: 0 with a town of a people at peace with the colony within 12 tiles, rising evenly to 1 at 40 tiles, and 0.2 more with fewer than two such towns within 40 tiles. It is worked out each day and falls by itself as the region fills. The region map shows it for a home in words, from close to its neighbors to far from everyone.

li.heading: Travelers who seek out the remote
li.text: The more remote a home, the more travelers seek it out. At the most remote, camps come up to 60% more often (a daily chance of 8 in 100 instead of 5) with up to 30% less rest after each, and Rimfolk's visitors up to 60% more often; on Rimfolk's own timer the wait between its events is cut by the visitors' share alone, so every other kind of event comes as often as before. A kind of camp that seeks what the land near the home has is up to three times as likely there, and says why it came: a relic of the colony's faith, a landmark, a great tree, ancient ruins on the colony's land or the ruins of a town in the region, the colony's books (six or more), its history (a year old, with five milestones), ore in sight, a rush, grass in its season, a road, or the distance from every market. Scholars come only for such a reason. A kind with no reason here comes as it always did.
li.after: Travelers tell news of towns beyond the region at their fire, two pieces a stay at most, each to a colonist sitting with them: a world event among a people, a war begun or ended lately, a new town, a site near it, a quest of theirs, never the same news of a town twice in ten days. It goes into that town's Heard lately, the history and the colony news. The region map's panel for a home says how much more often travelers come and what draws them, and lists the latest word from far towns. The setting Travelers to the remote (0 to 200%) scales all of it; at 0 nothing changes and no far news is told, though a camp still says why it came. The rates also need Systems talk to each other.

li.heading: Titles and rites in invitations
li.text: An invitation to a feast, midwinter or a wedding at a people's town comes from its head as the colony knows them, by the title the game shows them: an Empire head as baron or countess. A colonist who holds a title of the Empire is named first among the guests when the Empire invites. The invitation says how the day is kept: with Ideology, a ritual their faith really has (a feast, a wedding, a funeral), by its name; otherwise their age's way, a gift feast, a hunt and a tournament, a banquet, vows in the hall and a dowry. A people's asks for goods for a funeral or a wedding name their rite the same way.

li.heading: What their people remember, in events
li.text: Rimfolk's events about a people (visitors, callers, traders, their asks) read what that people remembers of the colony: the good turn they remember best ("among them, the colony is known as the place that set Ana free"), the wrong they remember worst, a favour they owe, and how their town is doing. A letter says so only when it is true.

li.heading: Towns that rise and fall
li.text: A town within reach that has struggled for a month (under 15), or was struck twice in a season by bad news of its people while under 25, or met a hard first season (under 10 in its first 15 days), may be given up: on a roll of 7 in 100 every five days, while its people keep two other towns, never their seat or the Empire's, and never a town the colony has business with (its map open, a quest about it, a caravan or pods on the way, a caravan request open). When a world event's slot is free it comes as a world event on that town, told by what struck it: a family of theirs may stop at the gate, what the town leaves behind is anyone's to take, and if the colony still has business there at the end a few families hold on. Otherwise the colony news says its families are on the road, a family of theirs may make camp at the gate (only while their people are at peace with the colony), and five days later the town is a ruin. Notables of the town the colony dealt with move to their people's nearest town.

table.li: Change | At most, in a home's reach | Its roll
A town given up | One in 60 days | 7 in 100, every 5 days
A ruin settled again | One in 120 days | 10 in 100, every 15 days
A town founded by Rimfolk | One in 90 days, while fewer than 10 towns stand in reach | 15 in 100, every 15 days
A ruin Rimfolk made | Twelve, the oldest going first | Gone after 300 days

li.after: A ruin is the game's own abandoned settlement, in its people's colour; its panel on the region map and its inspect pane say what town it was and how it came to this, in its people's age: empty longhouses and cold hearths, an empty town, a ghost town, a derelict colony. Where a fight destroys a town within reach, the game leaves nothing: Rimfolk puts a ruin on the tile once the destroyed settlement's map is gone, unless something else stands there by then. A ruin 120 days old may be settled again by a people at peace with the colony with a town within 25 tiles standing at 60 or more, or by its own people at 50: they come back under its old name, newcomers half the time under their own. A town flourishing (80 or more) for 60 days may send settlers out to found a town 6 to 15 tiles from it, on land where the game would put a town (more often where its land is kindly), never in another people's territory or beside a town being built. Nothing Rimfolk places stands within 6 tiles of any of the colony's settlements, where the game would hold the town's nearness against the colony. Each new town gets its founder and families, the colony news says how it came about, and the history keeps every change. Rimfolk's world events that give a town up or found one count on the same clocks.

A town's fortune reaches the colony too, with Systems talk to each other on: a people on good terms whose town in reach struggles asks for provisions and for help rebuilding twice as often, in that town's name; a call to shelter refugees comes twice as often when the people they flee from have a town struggling in reach; and a refugee family's camp is twice as likely, most likely of that people. Their trader caravans come a quarter more often while their town nearest the colony thrives or flourishes, and 0.6 as often while it struggles (with the deeper game hooks).

li.heading: Trading posts
li.text: A people at peace with the colony, with goodwill 40 or more (or allied), who have traded with it three times or more in the last 120 days, whose nearest town is 15 tiles or more from a home and who keep town traders (the Empire too), may open a trading post near that home. Each home is looked at every 15 days, with a 20% chance when such a people is there, the one that trades most first: two posts a home at most, one per people, none within 60 days of another opening or closing there. The post stands 6 to 12 tiles from the home, toward their nearest town (within 60 degrees) where it can, on a road (three times as likely) or a river (twice) by preference, on land that holds a town, 3 tiles or more from any other town and never within 6 tiles of a colony. With no such place, no post.

table.li: Their age | The post | Its keeper
Tribal | A trading camp | Their trader
Medieval | A market | Their factor
Industrial | A depot | Their manager
Spacer and the Empire | A ground station | Their quartermaster (an Empire keeper also carries a title of the Empire's own)

li.after: It is their town in every way: a caravan (or transport pods) trades there in the game's own trade window, quests may pick it, and it can be attacked. Its fortune starts at 40 and stays at 70 or under. Its keeper and its trader are among the notables at once, so letters to them travel only a few days, and the letter that opens it looks at it. While it stands, their trader caravans are half again as likely to be the ones that come, and the bandit road is twice as likely (both with Systems talk to each other; the caravans also with the deeper game hooks). With Faction Territories it is simply their town: their territory reaches toward the colony from it, and a post bought as the colony's vassal is a post no more.

When their goodwill has been under 0 for ten days, its keeper writes that it will close unless things mend; back at 0 or more, it stays, and the keeper says so. Still under 0 ten days after the warning, it closes through the region's giving up: its notables move to their people's nearest town and a ruin stands in its place. War with the colony closes it within a day. A post the colony has business with (a caravan or pods on the way, a quest, its map open) closes only once that is done. If their people are at war with a people whose town is within 20 tiles of it, raiders may sack it, 5 in 100 every 15 days: it loses 30 of its fortune, or, when that would leave it under 10, its people give it up and a family of theirs may make camp at the colony's gate. A post its people give up in hard times, as any town in reach may be, closes in the posts' history too. A post the colony razes is a heavy wrong their people remember, beside the game's own for a town destroyed. The region map's Trade lens shows each post, and its list how the last ones went, and This week shows a post whose keeper has warned. The setting Trading posts switches it off: no post opens, and those standing are ordinary towns of theirs.

li.heading: Settlers' hamlets
li.text: From the colony's 90th day, with five grown colonists or more at a home, settlers of a people at peace with the colony may ask to found a hamlet near it under its protection, at most once a year and one hamlet a home: a holding that has lived a year on the colony's land with little unease and wants a place of its own, the families of a town given up (the colony may offer them a place at its gate, beside taking them in), or settlers from a poor or struggling town in reach. Each home is looked at every 10 days, with a 15% chance when settlers qualify. Their letter shows the place they have in mind, 6 to 10 tiles off by the trading posts' rules, by a river or a road where it can; the colony may choose another place on the world map, held to the same rules.

table.li: The answer | What follows

Take them under protection and escort them | They camp by the colony with their carts for a few days; a caravan of two grown colonists or more sent to the place takes them along, beside it and named in its panel. After a night there with the caravan, the first fires are lit and the hamlet stands, its fortune from 25.
Let them go alone | They set off by themselves: a third are turned back on the road, and the rest found the hamlet with what the road left them, its fortune from 12.
Refuse | They look for a place elsewhere.

li.after: The hamlet is a town of the settlers' own people in every way, which follows them in war and peace: their leader is its head among the notables, their families its founding families, and a tie of fealty binds it to the colony. On arriving with the caravan, the road brings the game's own caravan demand or ambush 15 times in 100 (35 near a raiders' camp, or with a town of a hostile people within 15 tiles of the place), and the settlers' grown folk stand with the caravan when the attackers are their enemies too. Those of the colony who walked them out are remembered by name by their people.

At harvest a carter brings some of its produce to the colony's gate, with a little goodwill. In a hard season (its fortune under 20) it asks for food, a doctor's medicine or tools by the colony's means, carried down to their carter at the gate; help lifts its fortune by 6, and refused twice in one season it stops counting on the colony and the tie is broken. After 60 days at a fortune of 40 or more, with no ask refused in the last 60 days, it asks to swear fealty by its people's ways (gifts at the river, an oath before witnesses, a signed agreement, a registered charter). With Faction Territories' vassalage on, it becomes that mod's vassal of the colony's; otherwise it stays a town of its people, sworn to the colony. If its people turn on the colony first, its families choose: come to the colony (some of them join it, and the hamlet is given up when it can be), or stay with their people. At the end of its second year, it may grow into a town in its own right. The region map's Ours lens shows it, and This week shows settlers waiting at the gate. The setting Hamlets switches it off.

li.heading: Small towns look small
li.text: When the map of a hamlet, a trading post or a town in its first year is made, because the colony attacks it or a caravan enters it, its base is smaller and fewer defend it, so what the words call a hamlet is a hamlet. With Vanilla Base Generation Expanded each people's own layouts are built on the smaller ground. An Empire town keeps its ground with fewer defenders, and sites, ruins and other mods' world objects are never touched. The setting Small towns' maps switches it off (it needs the deeper game hooks).

table.li: The town | Its ground on each side | Its defenders | Its stores
A hamlet | 0.6 of a town's, and no walls | 0.35 of a town's | 0.4 of a town's
A trading post | 0.75 | 0.5 | 0.75
A town in its first year | 0.8 | 0.65 | 0.6

li.heading: With and without other mods
li.text: With Faction Territories and Vassalage, its builders give most new towns (each people one about every 30 days somewhere in its territory, ten days to build), and Rimfolk gives those within reach their faces; a town taken in one of its invasions starts its fortune again. Rimfolk founds its own towns beside them at its own pace, and its builders' sites and territories are left alone. Without it, new towns come from Rimfolk's world events and its own foundings. Real Ruins may dress a ruin Rimfolk made as it does any abandoned settlement; its own sites are left alone. The settings in The region switch the fortunes, their say in the trade stock, the new towns' faces and towns rising and falling off: then nothing is moved, made or told, and what is kept stays.
